speaker: Matt Risinger
title: Building Science with Matt Risinger ECP 66
question: In custom home construction, what happens financially to the general contractor when a client pushes for the cheapest waterproofing approach?
guest: I all the time get people that will say, "Oh, this is too expensive," or "This detail's too much." Well, if it's a water-related detail, it needs to be whatever is the right detail for the house, and your client needs to pay for it. Because if your client doesn't pay for it or can't afford to do that detail, how are they going to afford to redo it in three years when you're getting sued? You're going to pay for it, not your client. On one of my first client jobs in Texas, my client said, "You've got to get three bids on every phase." So I took the lowest roofing bidder. That roofer went out of business about six months after I finished the job. By the time I realized every scupper was leaking and we had to rip the roof off, he was long gone—he had no insurance, he was out of business. It was 100% on me. It cost me $30,000 to rip off that entire roof and redo it correctly with the next more expensive bidder, which I paid for, not my client.

points.core: When cheap water details fail years later, the general contractor absorbs replacement costs.
points.note: Accept: the GC ends up paying out of pocket to tear out and redo failed waterproofing properly, often at higher cost than doing it right upfront. Do not credit: generic advice not to cut corners without identifying who bears the financial loss.

points.note: Accept: even when the homeowner pushed to save money initially, they hold the builder legally and financially responsible when leaks surface years later. Do not credit: vague mentions of unhappy clients or bad reviews without legal/redo liability.

points.core: Lowest-bid subcontractors often go out of business before major waterproofing failures surface.
points.note: Accept: underpriced trades are financially fragile, frequently fold or disappear within months, or carry no valid insurance by the time latent leaks require remediation. Do not credit: generic claims that cheap subs do sloppy work without the post-completion disappearance/insolvency dynamic.

points.core: Subcontractor insolvency shifts full tear-off remediation expenses onto the general contractor.
points.note: Accept: with the low-bid sub gone or uninsured, 100% of warranty/remediation liability defaults back onto the GC. Do not credit: surface keyword mentions of insurance or warranties without the liability transfer to the GC.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The contractor usually ends up holding the risk while the client keeps the savings. Choosing the cheapest waterproofing (for example, basic damp-proofing spray instead of a full membrane with drainage board and proper footing drains) might save the client a few thousand dollars up front, but the contractor's liability does not shrink with the budget. Water intrusion is among the most common and expensive construction defect claims, and the builder generally remains responsible under implied warranties of workmanship and habitability and under statutes of repose that can run six to twelve years depending on the state.

If the system fails, the fix means excavation, tearing out finished interiors and mold remediation, often costing tens of thousands of dollars against a margin on the original work of a few hundred. Callbacks eat profit directly, insurance may exclude or only partly cover the claim, premiums rise, and reputation suffers.

That is why experienced builders either refuse to go below a minimum specification, price the risk in, or get the client's decision documented in a signed change order or waiver. Even then, a waiver offers limited protection, especially where the result falls below code.

models.answer: When a custom home client pushes for the cheapest waterproofing, the general contractor absorbs severe, one-sided financial risk while the client captures the upfront savings. Under a cost-plus contract, cutting waterproofing scope actually reduces the builder’s fee, and under a fixed-price contract, the credit goes to the owner—yet the builder still owns the failure risk. Even if the client signs a waiver, courts and state laws rarely allow contractors to disclaim building code compliance, statutory or implied warranties of habitability, or claims from subsequent homebuyers. Because waterproofing sits buried behind backfill, tile, or cladding, a leak requires demolishing and rebuilding expensive finished work, turning modest upfront savings into tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in remediation that can wipe out the entire project’s profit margin. Worse, general liability policies typically exclude repairing the defective work itself and often limit water or mold coverage, leaving the contractor paying out of pocket for callbacks, deductibles, legal defense, higher future premiums, and lost referrals—unless they refuse the shortcut upfront.

noweb.answer:
When a custom home client insists on the cheapest waterproofing, the general contractor absorbs severe, asymmetric financial risk for virtually no upside. In the short term, cutting that budget slightly shrinks the builder’s fee on a cost-plus contract while offering no protection on a fixed-price bid. The real financial blow arrives post-occupancy, because statutory warranties and implied habitability laws typically hold the contractor liable for water intrusion—even if the client requested the downgrade or signed a waiver. 

When cheap membranes, minimal flashing, or basic damp-proofing fail, repairs require excavating landscaping, demolishing finished siding, drywall, or custom flooring, remediating mold, and rebuilding at the contractor’s expense. Post-completion water remediation routinely costs ten to twenty times the initial savings, easily erasing the entire project profit and pushing the job into a deep net loss. Beyond direct callback expenses, water claims trigger steep insurance deductibles, legal fees, surging general liability premiums or policy non-renewal, and reputational damage that costs future contracts in a referral-driven market.

Saving a few thousand dollars on membranes, flashing or below-grade waterproofing does little for the contractor's margin. That bill tends to land on the builder. Implied warranties of workmanship and habitability, state statutory warranties and long repose periods (often around 10 years) can keep the contractor liable for years. A signed waiver from the client often doesn't hold up, especially if the work fell below code, the manufacturer's instructions or the standard of care. It also may not bind later buyers.

Insurance offers limited protection. Many general liability policies exclude faulty workmanship, mold or water intrusion, and claims push premiums up. Warranty callbacks consume overhead, and the hit to the builder's reputation can cost future referrals. For these reasons, experienced builders either refuse to go below a minimum standard or document the client's choice carefully in a formal change order. They also often price in a contingency for the extra risk.
